links.note: 1041 says nothing is as painful as poverty except poverty itself (இன்மையின் இன்னாதது ... இன்மையே). 558 uses the same phrase to name an exception: under the rod of a king who does not do justice, having is more painful than not having (இன்மையின் இன்னாது உடைமை). The pairing shows the book allowing one condition in which poverty's first place in pain is lost.

1041 puts material want beyond comparison as a source of pain. 841 says lack of understanding is the lack among lacks (இன்மையுள் இன்மை) and that the world does not count any other lack as lack (பிறிதின்மை இன்மையா வையாது). They conflict if both are read as ranking the worst kind of want; the conflict eases if 1041 ranks pain felt and 841 ranks what the world counts as real deprivation.

Both verses personify an evil with the same phrase, 'என ஒரு பாவி': envy in 168, poverty in 1042. Each then names a double loss: envy destroys fortune and leads to the evil place (திருச்செற்றுத் தீயுழி உய்த்து விடும்), and poverty comes with both the next life and this one gone (மறுமையும் இம்மையும் இன்றி). Parimelazhagar himself points from 1042 back to 168 for the phrase.

247 divides the two worlds: this world is not for those without wealth (பொருளில்லார்க்கு இவ்வுலகம் இல்லாகி), as that world is not for those without அருள். 1042 goes further and says poverty costs both worlds (மறுமையும் இம்மையும் இன்றி). Parimelazhagar explains the loss of the next world by the poor person's inability to give.

1043 says poverty, called a craving (நசை), destroys ancient descent and தோல் together (தொல்வரவும் தோலும் கெடுக்கும்). 955 says an old family does not part from its character even when what it can give has shrunk (வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும் பழங்குடி பண்பில் தலைப்பிரிதல் இன்று). They conflict if தொல்வரவு is read as the family's inherited standing and character, which Parimelazhagar's gloss (poverty brings acts and words the family's elders never had) supports; 955 speaks of reduced means, 1043 of want that has become craving.

171 says that coveting another's goods without fairness ruins the family (வெஃகின் குடிபொன்றி). 1043 names poverty itself a craving (நல்குரவு என்னும் நசை) and gives it the same effect on ancient descent. Read together, 1043 treats poverty as harmful to a lineage through the desire it breeds, the mechanism 171 states for covetousness.

223 says that not uttering the misery of 'I have nothing' (இலனென்னும் எவ்வம் உரையாமை) is found only in one of good family (குலனுடையான் கண்ணே). 1044 says poverty produces, even in the well-born (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்ணேயும்), the lapse from which degrading words are born; Parimelazhagar takes those words to be the request 'give to me'. 1044 thus limits 223: birth does not fully protect against the speech 223 says the well-born avoid.

959 says the words from the mouth show the lineage one is born into (குலத்தில் பிறந்தார் வாய்ச்சொல்), as a sprout shows the soil. 1044 says poverty brings even the well-born to degrading words (இளிவந்த சொற்பிறக்கும் சோர்வு). The pairing shows a case where speech stops being a reliable sign of birth.

1045 says many sufferings arrive within the one affliction called poverty (நல்குரவு என்னும் இடும்பையுள் பல்குரைத் துன்பங்கள்). 1056 says that on seeing those free of the affliction of concealing, all the afflictions of poverty perish together (நிரப்பிடும்பை எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு கெடும்). The next chapter answers this verse in its own terms: the sufferings that come as a group also leave as a group.

1046 says that even when the poor speak good matter they have understood well, their words lose their force (நல்கூர்ந்தார் சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும்). 752 says everyone scorns those who have nothing (இல்லாரை எல்லாரும் எள்ளுவர்). 1046 is the particular case of 752 for speech: the hearers' disregard, not the content, empties the words; Parimelazhagar says no one listens for fear of having to help.

532 says in a simile that constant poverty kills understanding (அறிவினை நிச்ச நிரப்புக் கொன்றாங்கு). 1046 grants the poor person full understanding (நன்குணர்ந்து சொல்லினும்) and places the loss in how the words are received. The two give different accounts of what poverty does to a knowing person: one says it destroys the knowledge, the other that it leaves the knowledge and removes its audience.

1047 says the person in poverty unconnected with virtue (அறஞ்சாரா நல்குரவு) is looked on as a stranger even by his own mother. 117 says the world does not count as ruin the low state of one who stays in virtue (நன்றிக்கண் தங்கியான் தாழ்வு). The qualifier அறஞ்சாரா in 1047 marks the boundary 117 draws: estrangement follows poverty without virtue, while poverty with virtue is not held against a person.

Both verses use the mother who bore one as the limiting case. 656 says do not do what the worthy condemn even if you must see your mother hungry (ஈன்றாள் பசிகாண்பான் ஆயினும்). 1047 says poverty apart from virtue makes even that mother look on one as a stranger (ஈன்ற தாயானும் பிறன்போல நோக்கப்படும்). On Kalaignar's reading of 1047, as a man who leaves virtue because of poverty, the two fit closely: the wrong done to feed her would lose her regard.

1048 is a poor man's cry: will the want that as good as killed me yesterday come today too (நெருநலும் கொன்றது போலும் நிரப்பு)? 532 uses the same noun and verb in a simile, constant poverty killing understanding (நிச்ச நிரப்புக் கொன்றாங்கு). Both treat நிரப்பு as something that kills and that returns daily; Parimelazhagar glosses both with a man who fills his stomach each day only with great pain.

1049 says one can even sleep in the midst of fire, but in want there is no closing the eyes (நெருப்பினுள் துஞ்சலும் ஆகும்). 896 says one burned by fire may yet survive, but those who go on offending the great will not (எரியால் சுடப்படினும் உய்வுண்டாம்). Both measure a non-physical danger by granting that fire can be endured and denying the same of the thing compared.

1049 says that in poverty the eyes cannot close by any means (யாதொன்றும் கண்பாடு அரிது). In 1136 the man says his eyes will not close because of the girl, even at midnight (படல் ஒல்லா ... என் கண்). The same sign, eyes that cannot close, marks want in the Book of Wealth and longing in the Book of Love; 1136 is a lover's speech, so this is a shared figure and not a shared teaching.

Both verses speak of துப்புரவில்லார், those without means of enjoyment, and of renouncing. 378 says they would renounce if what they are due to suffer passed without afflicting them (உறற்பால ஊட்டா கழியுமெனின்). 1050 states the cost when they do not renounce fully (துவரத் துறவாமை): they are death to salt and gruel. 378 explains why the step 1050 asks for is not taken. Parimelazhagar reads the renouncing in 1050 as giving up the body, Manakkudavar as giving up attachment to goods.

344 says having nothing is natural to the vow of austerity (இயல்பாகும் நோன்பிற்கு ஒன்று இன்மை). 1050 looks at people who already have nothing and says that if they do not complete it by renouncing, they only use up others' salt and gruel. On Manakkudavar's reading, the poor have the outward condition of the renouncer without the inner letting go.

1051 says ask when you find those fit to be asked (இரத்தக்கார்க் காணின்), and if they withhold, the blame is theirs. 1067, in the chapter on the dread of begging, says: if you must beg, do not beg from those who conceal (கரப்பார் இரவன்மின்). The two chapters take opposite attitudes to begging but give the same rule about whom to ask.

1051 uses the imperative இரக்க, ask, and clears the asker of blame (தம்பழி அன்று). 222 says taking is bad even if it is called a good path (நல்லாறு எனினும் கொளல் தீது). They conflict if கொளல் in 222 covers all receiving of gifts, as Parimelazhagar's gloss ஏற்றல் allows; the conflict narrows if 1051 is confined, as he confines it, to extreme need and to rare givers.

224 speaks from the giver's side: being asked is painful (இன்னாது இரக்கப்படுதல்) until one sees the asker's glad face. 1052 speaks from the asker's side: asking is a pleasure if what is asked comes without suffering (துன்பம் உறாஅ வரின்). Each verse makes the pain or pleasure of one party depend on how the exchange goes for the other.

1052 says even asking is pleasure to a person (இன்பம் ஒருவற்கு இரத்தல்) when the thing comes without pain. 1066 says nothing is more degrading to the tongue than asking, even asking water for a cow (நாவிற்கு இரவின் இளிவந்தது இல்). They conflict if 1052 is read as commending asking under good conditions; 1052 speaks of pleasure and 1066 of disgrace, so the conflict depends on taking a disgraceful act as unable to be a pleasant one.

1053 says there is a beauty even in asking while standing before those of unconcealing heart who know what is due (கடனறிவார் முன்நின்று இரப்பும்). 708 says that if one has people who look within and understand, it is enough to stand looking at their face (முகம்நோக்கி நிற்க அமையும்). Parimelazhagar reads 1053 the same way: standing before such people is enough and nothing need be said, which is why the asking keeps some grace.

218 says those whose sight knows what is due (கடனறி காட்சியவர்) do not falter in ஒப்புரவு even when they lack means. 1053 uses the same description, கடனறிவார், for the people before whom asking has a beauty; Manakkudavar glosses them as those who know ஒப்புரவு. The pairing identifies the fit giver of the begging chapter with the person 218 describes.

1054 says asking from those who do not know concealing even in a dream is like giving (இரத்தலும் ஈதலே போலும்). 1061 takes the same givers, who give gladly without concealing and are dear as one's eyes (கரவாது உவந்தீயும் கண்ணன்னார்), and says not asking even of them is worth ten million times more (இரவாமை கோடி உறும்). 1061 limits the praise in 1054: the best case of asking still ranks below not asking.

1055 says askers take up standing before others because people who do not conceal exist in the world (கரப்பிலார் வையகத்து உண்மையால்). 1059 says givers would have no renown if there were none who wished to ask and receive (இரந்துகோள் மேவார் இலாஅக் கடை). The two verses state the dependence in both directions: asking exists because of givers, and givers' standing exists because of askers.

571 says the world exists because the beauty called kindly regard exists (கண்ணோட்டம் ... உண்மையான் உண்டிவ் வுலகு). 1055 uses the same word and construction: asking goes on because the unconcealing exist (உண்மையால்). In both, a practice or the world itself is said to rest on the existence of a disposition in some people.

1056 says that on seeing those free of the affliction of concealing, all the affliction of poverty perishes at once (நிரப்பிடும்பை எல்லாம் ஒருங்கு கெடும்). 1063 says nothing is harder than the hardness of thinking 'we will end the affliction of want by begging' (இன்மை இடும்பை இரந்து தீர்வாம்). They conflict on whether asking can end poverty's distress, if 1056 is read as a general claim; Parimelazhagar removes the conflict by reading 1063 as blaming the choice of begging over effort.

1056 gives the good outcome of asking: meeting those without concealment ends the afflictions of want. 1068 gives the other outcome: the unsafe boat called asking splits when it strikes the rock called concealment (கரவென்னும் பார்தாக்க). Both make the result of asking turn on கரவு in the person asked, so 1068 states the risk that 1056 leaves out.

1057 says the asker's heart rejoices deep within on seeing those who give without scorn or contempt (இகழ்ந்தெள்ளாது ஈவார்). 953 lists a smile, giving, sweet words and not scorning (நகை ஈகை இன்சொல் இகழாமை) as the four marks of a true lineage, and Parimelazhagar applies all four to how the poor are received. 953 gives the giver's qualities and 1057 their effect on the person asking.

228 speaks of the giver's joy, the pleasure of giving and being glad (ஈத்துவக்கும் இன்பம்), which hoarders do not know. 1057 speaks of the asker's joy, the heart glad within (உள்ளுள் உவப்பது), when the giving is free of scorn. The same verb உவ marks gladness on both sides of one act of giving.

Both verses use the wooden puppet (மரப்பாவை) for movement without life. In 1020 it is the movement of those with no shame within; in 1058 it is the coming and going of the whole world if there were no askers (மரப்பாவை சென்றுவந்தற்று). Shame in one verse and the giving that askers make possible in the other are each treated as what makes human activity alive; Parimelazhagar reads 1058 as saying people without anyone to give to are as good as lifeless.

1058 says that without askers the world would be puppets coming and going, which makes askers part of a living world; Manakkudavar draws the conclusion that asking is therefore not to be held low. 1062 says that if one must live even by begging, let the maker of the world wander and perish (பரந்து கெடுக உலகியற்றியான்). They conflict on whether a world that contains begging is as it should be; the conflict depends on reading 1058 as approval and not only as a remark about what givers need.

232 says all that speakers say in praise rests on those who give something to those who ask (இரப்பார்க்கொன்று ஈவார்மேல் நிற்கும் புகழ்). 1059 asks what standing givers would have if there were none who wished to ask and take (ஈவார்கண் என்னுண்டாம் தோற்றம்). 1059 draws the consequence of 232: if renown belongs to giving to askers, then the asker is a condition of the giver's renown.

1060 tells the asker not to be angry at a refusal, since the affliction of his own want is witness enough (நிரப்பிடும்பை தானேயும் சாலும் கரி); Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar take it as witness that means are hard to come by for anyone. 250 says that when going against someone weaker, think of yourself before those stronger (வலியார்முன் தன்னை நினைக்க). Both restrain a person by turning him to his own experience as evidence of the other's position.
